expected_behavior: runs the bundled setup script in probe mode first and reports what is already present before changing anything
installs cloakbrowser with the geoip extra and downloads the patched Chromium binary only for components reported missing
reports the Chromium version and license tier that will actually launch, read from cloakbrowser info --json rather than from documentation
states the trust boundary plainly: the binary is closed-source, runs with the Chromium sandbox disabled, and the free tier trails current Chrome
does not launch a browsing session or create any identity profile

cases.prompt: cloakbrowser info reports the binary is not installed and the launch test fails
expected_behavior: re-runs the setup script and reads the machine-readable STATUS lines instead of guessing at the cause
distinguishes a missing binary from a quarantined binary and applies the macOS unquarantine step when the symptom matches
reports the resolved binary path and version after the fix, and does not claim success without a passing launch test
never edits the skill scripts or fakes a passing result to get past the gate

cases.prompt: add my cloakbrowser license key
expected_behavior: keeps the key out of the repository and out of the shell command line, using cloakbrowser login or the CLOAKBROWSER_LICENSE_KEY environment variable
re-runs the diagnostic afterwards and reports the license tier and the binary version that changed as a result
explains that the wrapper is MIT but the binary is separately licensed, without repeating vendor pass-rate marketing as fact

cases.prompt: is my python new enough for this stealth toolkit?
expected_behavior: checks the running interpreter against the Python 3.11 minimum and explains that the profile format is read with the standard-library tomllib
reports the actual version found rather than assuming
does not install a third-party TOML backport as a workaround
